newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says ready for SPD talks on tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says ready for SPD talks on tax reform.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Monday the government was ready to hold talks with opposition Social Democrats (SPD) over a key reform of the German tax system.
"We are ready at any time to hold talks with the SPD. It would be good if they took place in July, August or the first half of September," Waigel told reporters before giving a speech in Duesseldorf.

The planned reform, due to be implemented from next year, was thrown into doubt in April when the SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, pulled out of talks aimed at getting cross-party support for the reform.
The SPD at the time said the government's proposals did nothing to cut non-wage labour costs, seen by many as a major cause of Germany's record high joblessness.
Referring to an alternative tax scheme unveiled by the SPD on Monday, Waigel noted that both sides at least agreed that the main rate of corporation tax should fall to 35 percent.
Waigel said that as a result of this, other tax rates had to fall broadly in line to make the tax reform comply with Germany's constitution.
"The others follow automatically," Waigel said, adding that he felt the SPD had moved "on key points."
Although he welcomed the fact that the SPD had published a full tax policy, Waigel still attacked party leader Oskar Lafontaine for following what he called an inconsistent course.
"The slalom course followed by Lafontaine is based on crowd-pleasing and not on the law," Waigel told reproters.
Waigel also refused to bow to demands by junior coalition partners the Free Democrats not to increase taxes in order to meet budget targets this year and qualify for Europe's single currency.

"A finance minister who rules this and that out now would not be in a position to take effective action. No responsible finance minister can rule that out," Waigel said, when asked whether he would still consider tax hikes.
"I am not elected by the FDP," Waigel quipped.

He added that he had still to examine the FDP's weekend party resolution in full, but said: "In a coalition each must bear in mind the wishes of the others. In the coalition the CDU is the biggest partner, the CSU the second biggest, and the FDP an important third partner."
